content: In settings where a high number of cesarean sections are presumed to be unnecessary, the proportion of births resulting from such unnecessary procedures was not reported in the studies reviewed. For instance, it remains unclear whether the cesarean section rates observed after educational interventions were due to unnecessary procedures or whether cesarean sections might have been appropriate for women who ultimately had vaginal births. This uncertainty necessitates caution when interpreting the recommendations provided in this guideline. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) issued five recommendations focused on non-clinical interventions aimed at reducing unnecessary cesarean sections. These interventions should be implemented alongside other proven strategies to enhance the quality of care for mothers and newborns during childbirth. The recommendations are categorized based on the target audience: (a) interventions directed at women, (b) interventions directed at healthcare professionals, and (c) interventions directed at health organizations, facilities, or systems. Evidence supporting the effectiveness of these interventions was derived from an updated Cochrane review of 29 studies, including 19 randomized controlled trials, one controlled before-and-after study, and nine interrupted time series studies. Most of these studies (20 out of 29) were conducted in high-income countries, with none performed in low-income settings. The studies spanned 16 countries, including the United States, Canada, Finland, Portugal, Sweden, the United Kingdom, Chile, Brazil, Cuba, Guatemala, Mexico, Iran, China, Taiwan, and Australia. Descriptions of the interventions, their estimated effects, and certainty ratings (using the GRADE framework) are summarized in supplementary materials. Additionally, evidence from three systematic reviews of qualitative studies informed judgments about values, resource implications, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Overall, 49 studies (reported in 52 papers) were included in these reviews. Twelve studies explored the views and experiences of women, communities, and the public regarding non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. These studies were conducted in seven countries, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, Norway, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Eleven of these studies were from high-income countries, and one was from a middle-income country. Seventeen studies examined the perspectives of healthcare professionals on non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary cesarean sections. These studies were conducted in 17 countries, including Australia, Canada, China, Ethiopia, Finland, Germany, Ireland, Iran, Italy, Kenya, the Netherlands, Nicaragua, Sweden, Uganda, Tanzania, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Nine studies were from high-income countries, six from middle-income countries, and two from low-income countries. Twenty-five studies (reported in 28 papers) focused on non-clinical interventions targeting organizations, facilities, or health systems. These studies were conducted in 17 countries, including Bangladesh, Benin, Burkina Faso, Canada, Chile, China, Ghana, Iran, Japan, Lebanon, Mali, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Senegal, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Nine studies were from high-income countries, 11 from middle-income countries, and five from low-income countries. The GDG did not make recommendations for seven pre-specified guideline questions due to a lack of eligible studies. These questions have been proposed for future research. Non-Clinical Educational Interventions Recommendation 1: Health education for women is a critical component of antenatal care. The following educational interventions and support programs are recommended to reduce cesarean births, provided they are accompanied by targeted monitoring and evaluation (context-specific recommendation, low-certainty evidence): Childbirth training workshops Nurse-led applied relaxation training programs Psychosocial couple-based prevention programs Psychoeducation for women with a fear of childbirth Details of Interventions: 1. Childbirth Training Workshops: These workshops consisted of three four-hour weekly sessions in groups of 30 participants. Topics included fear and pain during childbirth, pharmacological and non-pharmacological pain relief techniques, advantages and disadvantages of cesarean and vaginal delivery, and indications/contraindications for cesarean sections. 2. Nurse-Led Applied Relaxation Training Program: This program involved seven 90-minute group education sessions over seven weeks, led by a nurse under the supervision of a clinical psychologist. Content included discussions on anxiety and stress during pregnancy, applied relaxation techniques, and deep breathing exercises. 3. Psychosocial Couple-Based Prevention Program: This program consisted of nine classes, with four weekly sessions during the second or third trimester of pregnancy and four weekly sessions within the first six months postpartum. Topics included emotional self-management, conflict resolution, problem-solving, communication, and mutual support strategies to foster positive joint parenting. 4. Psychoeducation for Women with Fear of Childbirth: This intervention involved six group sessions during pregnancy and one session with newborns six to eight weeks postpartum. Each two-hour session included a focused topic and a 30-minute guided relaxation exercise using an audio recording designed for this purpose. Topics covered included fear and anxiety, stages of labor, hospital routines, the birth process, and pain relief options. Women expressed a desire for educational tools such as workshops, booklets, and decision aids, delivered in multiple formats. They emphasized the importance of content that does not provoke anxiety and aligns with advice from healthcare professionals. Emotional support was also highlighted as a critical component alongside factual information. Evidence and Recommendations Evidence on non-clinical educational interventions targeted at women was derived from 15 randomized controlled trials included in the Cochrane review update. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries, with six studies from middle-income countries and none from low-income countries. The interventions assessed included childbirth training workshops, psychosocial couple-based prevention programs, pelvic floor muscle training with telephone follow-up, and psychoeducation for women with a fear of childbirth. Some interventions, such as childbirth training workshops and nurse-led relaxation programs, were found to reduce cesarean section rates. However, the effects of other interventions, such as prenatal education for partners or psychoeducation sessions by telephone, remain uncertain. Limited data were available on the impact of these interventions on maternal and neonatal mortality and morbidity. Resource Implications One study compared the cost of group psychoeducation with conventional care for women with a fear of childbirth in Finland. No significant differences were observed in total direct costs between the two groups. Key resource requirements for implementing these interventions include trained healthcare personnel, physical space for workshops, and educational materials in local languages.
